subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in connection with the caught-short statement he made last night in the House. Would he indicate the criteria which motivated the government's action in intervening in the case of Home Oil in contrast to earlier cases also involving foreign take-overs in which the government did not intervene? Can we also be told whether these same criteria will apply in future instances despite any recommendation which may be brought in by the Minister of National Revenue in his report on foreign ownership?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: We are, of course, awaiting the report of the Minister of National Revenue and government policy which will flow from it. At the present time there are no specific criteria concerning these matters; each case must be judged on its merits. Certainly one of the very important factors in this instance was, I think, the extremely good debate which took place in the House the other day and the very clear impression given by all members who spoke that the people of Canada, as represented by the members of this House, were very anxious that this company should be maintained as Canadian. I believe this House does represent, on these great national issues, the will of the people of Canada very clearly, and during the debate in question I think that will was made manifest very forcibly.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: That was quite a statement. Maybe my question will clarify it. Bearing in mind the fact that the government has intervened and declared its intention to purchase a controlling interest in Cygnus, thereby controlling Home Oil, may I ask whether the thousands of shareholders have been assured by the government that they will not be penalized as a result of this ad hoc decision? Further, would the minister tell us what price the government intends to pay for the shares, and how many shares it is purchasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: As to the details of the purchase, I do not think I would be serving the public interest by discussing them until the negotiations are completed one way or the other. With respect to the interest of the shareholders, I cannot believe that the purchase of Mr. Brown's holdings by the government of Canada or one of its agencies would be more detrimental to other shareholders than to have them purchased by a United States company.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: I do not think this question will prejudice anyone, Mr. Speaker. Is there at this stage a formal agreement or statement of intention on the part of the government to purchase Mr. Brown's controlling interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL
speechtext: I do not believe it would be advantageous, as I have said, to do our negotiating in public. Because of the great concern shown by the House with regard to this issue I did indicate as soon as I could the fact that the game had changed to the extent that the government was now negotiating. I thought I owed this courtesy to the House in view of the great interest displayed in the subject by hon. members. However, I do not think it would be useful to carry on the negotiations more publicly at this time.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS BY GOVERNMENT TO ACQUIRE CONTROLLING INTEREST IN HOME OIL

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (Peace River) moved:
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
That this House opposes the Trans-Alaska pipeline and tanker project because of the ecological dangers posed by this project to the people, towns, and cities of British Columbia and the national resources of Canada's western seas and coasts and that this House therefore urges the Government to immediately institute an independent economical and ecological feasibility study of alternative routes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has not been without some thought that this motion has been brought forward in order to provide hon. members of the House with an opportunity to express their views on this most important issue. We do not say that the importance of the issue transcends other considerations. It involves, to some extent, the question of the internal operations of another country. There are times, Mr. Speaker, when the representatives of the people must speak out loudly and clearly. We have been trying to force this government, which is or should be the natural guardian of the safety of our land and the organization responsible for securing the resources of the people in any part of this land, to act. The government has failed dismally to do anything other than bring forward pious proposals such as the one brought forward by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) when he said, "Yes, this is a serious problem; I invite all Canadians to write to the American government." More than that is involved. The people of Canada have a right to hear their government express its views. The government has refused to act. We shall see what the people of the country will think of what is said in the House today, because this House can and I hope will take a very positive position in supporting the motion.
We contemplated moving the motion as a non-confidence motion, because a great many members, some of whom are on the other side, have been very free with their comments. In our opinion, they would probably have considered very carefully how they would vote. We decided on the present form of the motion for the very simple reason that there ought to be no inhibitions in this debate. I hope that every hon. member in the House will support this motion.
This government has been undecided and has vacillated a good deal. When they come to the edge of the water, they shiver and tremble and are afraid to enter. Usually, at that point there is a flurry of contradictory statements by ministers. Some ministers have not harboured an unuttered thought in the House or outside on this issue; other ministers have never made a thoughtful utterance.
This has placed two, three or four ministers in a difficult and perplexing position, and it is partly for that reason we have brought forward the motion.
The motion begins in this way, "That this House opposes the Trans-Alaska pipeline and tanker project because of the ecological dangers posed," and so on. Let me say that so far as I am concerned, the question of the pipeline across Alaska lies exclusively and peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the United States government and the state of Alaska. There can be no doubt of that. We may have our views, and we have every right to say what dangers may be inherent in the construction of the pipeline, but the ultimate decision rests exclusively with the United States authorities.
At first blush we might say that the same objections apply to the further means of transporting oil from the Port of Valdez down to the Washington area, where the oil will be processed and refined. It is abundantly clear, I think, in view of the collisions between giant tankers which have caused immeasurable damage to the ecology, to the beaches and to the economies all over the world, that we face a particularly serious problem in this regard. Those matters have been mentioned from time to time in this House. No one will deny that the route to be utilized by these tankers, from Valdez down to the port in the state of Washington, is across dangerous waters. The final passage over the high seas, just before the ships come to port, will be particularly dangerous. The people of Canada in general, and the people on the west coast in particular, have a vested interest in the matter and a right to demand that their opposition to this means of transportation shall be expressed formally and categorically. If it is not expressed by the government, it certainly ought to be expressed by the members of this House.
The issue has been befogged by contradictory ministerial statements. Actually, a member on the government side from British Columbia said on television the other day that there should be a moratorium on ministerial statements. That is a good idea and ought to have been put into effect some time ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
These contradictory statements have not helped. It is not as if this were some new problem. For several months hon. members have been dealing with the matter in the form of questions, trying to get this slippery and devious government to answer, without any measure of success. There is a very distinguished member of the other place, the former premier of my province of Alberta. Aside from some of the defects he may have, he is one of the most knowledgeable persons in this country with regard to natural gas, oil and petroleum and the means of transporting them. On March 9, a few days ago, Senator Manning made a speech dealing with these issues. I wish to put on record some of the remarks made by this distinguished ornament of the other place with regard to this issue. At that time he was dealing with the bill before the Senate to amend the shipping act and establish a maritime pollu-

March 12, 1971

tion claims fund. We had already dealt with that in this House. He said:
On the other hand, perhaps the greatest single pollution threat to Canadian coastal waters will not arise at all from oil being imported into or exported from Canada, but from the offshore movement of oil between Alaska and the western parts of the United States.
He went on to say this should not have come as any surprise to the government because the last official representation which he made to the government of Canada when he was premier of Alberta had to do with this very matter. At page 651 of the Senate Hansard, he is reported as saying:
My representations to the federal Government were twofold. I urged, first of all, that immediate steps be taken, in advance of Alaskan oil coming into the world market picture, to ascertain as accurately as possible the impact that this new source of American oil supply could have on our economy, and especially on the petroleum industry in this country. Secondly, the view of the Government of Alberta at that time, was that it would be very much in Canada's interests to make representations to the United States to endeavour to interest them in moving that oil, as and when it did develop, by a pipeline through Canada to the main market areas of the Chicago region, rather than by the proposed pipeline across Alaska and by tanker down the Pacific coast to Seattle, and then back by pipeline to the Chicago area.
The government should have listened to this firm and definite caveat filed by this man two or three years ago. The advice was worth following. He knew what he was talking about. The then premier of Alberta laid down in plain terms the dangers and suggested alternatives.
The government has not done anything; it has failed to act. We will be faced with a crisis before we realize it. This government will not act. We in the Opposition are compelled to bring the matter forward in order to engage the attention of the public and secure the support of views which have been expressed.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
The United States has a very deep and vested interest in the Alaskan oil fields and the transportation of that oil to the centre of the continent. In rounded figures it is estimated that total U.S. consumption to date lies around 90 billion barrels, with existing conventional reserves pegged somewhere around 40 to 45 billion barrels, exclusive of Alaska oil. The present U.S. daily consumption lies somewhere near 12 to 13 million barrels. Furthermore, according to the U.S. interior department, over-all consumption of electricity rose 9.2 per cent in 1970 with petroleum supplying 43 per cent of all energy used. At a predicted increase of 4 per cent oil consumption per year, it becomes apparent that the U.S. needs Prudhoe Bay oil for its immediately foreseeable energy demands.
This is a fact we cannot change. We are a friendly neighbour, so we must contemplate their needs and requirements. They have secondary effects upon his country and our people. The government will not listen when we plainly and honestly say to them that there are inherent dangers in the proposed route, that there are alternatives
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
and that they should examine these alternatives. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) has indicated that certain studies may or will be made. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) is not quite as specific. I am inclined to accept at face value the views of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. However, he is only one member of the government.
We have had experience with this slippery and devious government. We do not believe them when they tell us what they are going to do. We had faith in them two and one half years ago, but that faith is gone.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
I am inclined to give credence to a newly elected government with a mandate. However, I simply cannot accept the fact that the government will do these things. The minister is doing what he can, but how long will he be in that position? There is the absolute necessity of firmly and irrevocably indicating what steps will betaken and how long it will take.
What are the alternatives? First, if any country has a vested interest, there should be some form of international discussion followed by a treaty and an arrangement. This country has petroleum and natural gas reserves on the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic coasts. Canada is a middle sized nation. Until the past year, it had a lot friends in the world. It is to our advantage to take the initiative to bring together the countries of the world which need to be involved in working out a long range plan for international control of pollution, particularly the oil pollution which is threatened by the proposal envisaged in the TAPS system of transporting Alaskan oil to the south. One of the ministers who will speak in this debate should make a categorical statement and give an undertaking that the government will, if it has not already done so, initiate this step. A firm commitment with regard to the type of international convention which I suggest is absolutely essential.
Apart from that, what are some of the problems which we face? First, there are the dangers which are to be found in the actual proposal for the TAPS line. A report was made by the United States Army Corps of Engineers which warns that they might prohibit construction of port facilities at Valdez. This is a statement by a responsible organization charged by a statute of the United States with certain responsibilities. If this proposal is considered dangerous by the United States army corps, it must be considered even more so by the people of British Columbia.
A study of future tanker traffic in Puget Sound by the Honeywell Corporation of Minneapolis has predicted two to four tanker collisions in this area in the next ten years. Furthermore, two experts who testified at the recent Anchorage-Washington meetings pointed out that one collision by a supertanker would turn that area of the west coast into a dead sea. Canada is concerned about possible serious oil pollution along the Pacific coast if the

March 12, 1971
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
tanker system is to be used. In addition, of course, there is the risk of damage to the ecology; we are sympathetic to the position taken by the conservationists who have voiced these fears at Anchorage but this, of course, is something which directly affects the people of the United States, particularly Alaska. In this connection there is also, of course, the knowledge that earthquakes are frequent in the area to be traversed by the proposed pipeline, but this question, too, lies within the jurisdiction of the American people.
Taking all these things into account, together with the growing knowledge which is becoming available to the people of the world as to what is happening to our environment, how could this Parliament possibly fail to express in the strongest terms its objection to the use of tankers to bring down oil from the north along the line which has been projected? I realize there will be other speakers in this debate and I do not intend to take up the full time allotted to me. But there are alternatives which have been considered.
There is the alternative of transportation through the Arctic sea, as illustrated by the experience of the Manhattan last year. I, myself, together with others in opposition parties, had occasion to express our objection to this being done in the absence of greater safeguards than were possible at that time. It would appear now, from the statement issued by the Humble Oil Company, that this project has been shelved. It was in connection with this voyage, however, that the government saw fit to bring before Parliament and have passed a bill dealing with the control of waters in the Arctic. That bill dealt with the control of Arctic waters within 100 miles of the edge of the Arctic archipelago. Although I had some doubts as to the possible legality of this legislation, although I doubted whether it was entirely necessary, I nevertheless, together with my hon. friends, gave the bill support. If the government can do this in the Arctic, Mr. Speaker, what inhibits it from making the strongest official representations with regard to the west coast, assuming, as I am assuming, that it would be doing so with the unanimous support of this House?
I need hardly point out that opinion in the United States is divided on this issue. The very fact that the program has been postponed for some time indicates that this is the case. It may well be that the United States government is just playing for time. In both nations there may be an election in 1972; it may even be that both governments concerned are trying to brush this issue under the carpet until the elections are over. I hope not, because if there is anything far too important to admit of playing politics it is pollution and, in particular, pollution caused by oil tanker collisions.
Then, there is the alternative of the Mackenzie route. This represents a difficult problem for Canadians, particularly those in the region which would be affected. We might be accused of opposing one solution in order to
secure an economic benefit from the other. But this is beside the point. There are people in this country, and I count myself among them, who would be completely opposed to the construction of a pipeline through any part of northern Canada until it had been shown clearly that such a pipeline could be built with a minimum of damage. It is unfortunate that this was not done a long time ago when the then premier of Alberta, Premier Manning, requested it. He stated, in language which could not be plainer: here is the problem, here are possible solutions; do something about it. Now, the government is in a position where it is called upon to act precipitously and, possibly, without the degree of care which is necessary. The Mackenzie route does provide a reasonable alternative provided a careful study is made beforehand and great care taken to avoid harmful effects. Other members of my party will be going into this in more detail.
I conclude on the following note: I do not think there is anything in the terms of this motion which should inhibit any member of the House giving it his undivided support. I wish it could be the subject of a vote in order that the government would be armed with an unanimous expression of support from this House of its determination to press forward with objection to the maritime part of the TAPS route. As it is, I hope the voice expressed here will be so strong and certain that the government will be obliged to act. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said this morning that the government had been greatly moved by the debate in this House on the question of Home Oil. I do not know whether or not he was speaking with his tongue in his cheek or not, but I will give him credit for meaning what he said. In the past, it has not seemed to me that the government has been particularly responsive to the mood of Parliament. If the government is prepared to take action on the basis of the views expressed here, then I hope the House speaks with such a loud, clear voice today that those sitting on the treasury benches will act in the way in which they are called upon to act by the terms of the motion before us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Official Opposition has put this motion down for discussion today. The general subject has received a certain amount of attention in recent weeks. Attempts have been made under Standing Order 43 to bring about a discussion of the subject mentioned in the first part of the motion. The first such attempt was made in a motion of my own by which this House would have put its stamp of approval on the opinion expressed unanimously in the British Columbia legislature against the idea of a massive movement of oil by large tankers down the Pacific coast of Canada.
The motion which the Conservatives have placed before us is capable of a natural division into two parts. I should like to comment on each of those parts. Part one exposes what I might call the ecological dangers of a Trans-Alaska pipeline and tanker route which would involve shipping large quantities of oil close to the west

March 12, 1971

coast of Canada. As hon. members know, this motion will not be brought to a conclusion by way of a formal expression of opinion by the House. I must say at once that I believe the position of the Official Opposition, let alone that of the government, would have been much more credible had they supported the amendment which I proposed not long ago to Bill C-2, to amend the Canada Shipping Act. This amendment would have asserted Canadian control over navigation to a distance of 100 miles from both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada. In the circumstances, I feel the Official Opposition has declined to take a firm position. Had they, and had the House as a whole, seen fit to adopt the amendment to which I have referred, the voice of Canada could have been much more definitely expressed to the world at large, including our neighbour to the south and to the north, since we are talking about Alaska.
As the question is put in this motion, we are still going to be left somewhat up in the air by the time the debate is over. It seems to me that in view of the fact we took a clear position in respect of the 100 mile jurisdiction proposal last year in the Arctic, while at the same time leaving unprovided for the similar ecological dangers posed to our Atlantic and Pacific Coasts, in some respects we have locked ourselves in, in the discussions that are now current concerning the movement of oil from the north slope of Alaska to the continental United States. I should like the House to recall that my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) attempted last year to include the provision of a 100 mile pollution control zone off our Atlantic and Pacific coasts, at the same time that we were indicating our strong support for the government's position on the Arctic.
So, first of all, my chief regret must be that by its initiative in the Arctic last year the government, and I suppose Parliament as a whole since we supported it, may very well have precipitated the situation which we are discussing with great concern today, namely the massive movement of oil along the Pacific coast of Canada. This must be my first comment on the motion, and in all fairness I must include, in my criticism of the way in which we are boxed in today, the official opposition as well as with the government. When it came to the crunch, both the government and the official opposition refused to take a firm and clear Canadian position on the need to protect the ecology along our Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
The second part of the motion suggests that this House should urge the government to immediately institute an independent economical and ecological feasibility study of all alternative routes. This raises many broad issues, as the hon. member for Peace River indicated. In the course of the discussions which took place last year a number of alternative routes were considered and examined, in a rather cursory fashion of course, including the transportation of oil across the Arctic by oil tanker. One of the committees heard quite extensive evidence as to the possibility of transporting oil under the Arctic ice pack by large submarine tankers. Incidentally, during
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
discussion of the Territorial Lands Act Amendments there was a good deal of discussion of the question of pipelines and their relationship to the ecology of the Canadian Arctic and, in particular, to that of the Mackenzie valley.
We now find ourselves in the position, because of the developments that have taken place in Alaska and the initiatives that have been taken in the United States, of being in danger of being stampeded into a quick decision, on the question of alternative routes, one which would be ecologically damaging and might not be in the long range interests of the Canadian economy.
The question I should like to ask in relation to the second part of this motion is this. For what purpose does the official opposition suggest that a study of alternate routes should be made? I listened carefully to the speech made by the hon. member for Peace River in introducing this motion, but I failed to detect any clear statement as to what should be the basic and underlying purpose of this study. Is this study to be undertaken for the convenience of the United States? Is its basic purpose to be to find for the United States some system of moving oil from Alaska to the southern part of their continental possessions without regard, except in a minor way, for the ecological consequences of an interior route through Canada? These are questions that have not been answered by spokesmen for the official opposition; nor indeed have they been answered in any way, shape or form to date by ministers of the government who have spoken in various ways and at various times, both inside and outside the House, on this particular subject.
About the only thing that we have had has been the picture of a couple of our ministers scurrying off to Texas to have some discussions with those people whom not too many years ago the then leader of the Conservative party described as "Texas buccaneers". Is this the place where the decision as to the future routing of oil from Alaska to the continental United States is going to be made, down in Texas with a few oil magnates? This is the impression that has been left in this House by the only definitive actions taken by the government to date, apart from the very nebulous comment made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that he hopes to have some kind of discussions with the Secretary of State of that country. These are the kinds of questions that we in this House should be asking ourselves in discussing a motion that suggests that a study concerning the economic and ecological feasibility of alternative routes be undertaken.
The question why we should undertake this study is one that I examined in my own mind as soon as I was acquainted with the contents of the motion that has been moved today. I propose to move an amendment to the motion which I hope will serve to focus attention on why a study should be undertaken on some real and basic issues as far as Canada and its future are concerned. I hope that when the spokesmen for the government reply they will relate their comments, in part at least, to the proposal I want to make. So that the House may clearly understand what I have in mind, I should like to move at

March 12, 1971
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
this point, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"with a view to developing under public ownership a transport system for oil and gas which will best serve the long-term interests of the Canadian economy".
If we are to undertake a study immediately, urgently and in depth, and in a way which will take into account all of the ramifications of this question for the purpose enunciated in this amendment, then let me say at once I am in full support of the proposal made by the official opposition. But I must say I am not too confident that the official opposition will agree with this particular approach as the basic reason for this proposal. I happened to come across an article in the Ottawa Citizen for March 10, 1971, written by Mr. Dave McIntosh. In this article he suggested that there may be another great pipeline debate shaping-up, with additional ingredients. I hope he does not mean that we are going to have the kind of parliamentary shambles associated with that earlier debate. I should like to suggest that the issues coming to the fore in relation to the transportation of petroleum products are even more basic and fundamental to the future of Canada as a country than the issues which were involved in that infamous pipeline debate. Mr. McIntosh says:
It was the NDP, then the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF), that began the big 1956 pipeline fight.
As I recall that debate, I cannot help but compare it in my own mind with the situation that prevails now. The focus of that debate as far as we were concerned was how the pipeline should be built. There is no question in my mind that there was anything but basic agreement on both sides of this House, certainly between CCF members and the minister who proposed this pipeline bill, that the destiny of Canada as a nation should be strengthened and made viable. I have always given the late C. D. Howe full credit for his efforts in this regard. We had little objection to his enunciated intention in respect of the construction of an all-Canadian pipeline. This was something we understood and supported. I have always been prepared to give him full credit in this regard because I think he was right.
I sometimes wonder what the reaction of the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe would be today if he were sitting in the gallery listening to the lily-livered, wishy-washy statements of policy we receive these days from members on the government benches? I am sure the late C. D. Howe would hoot in scorn and cry with derision at the concept of the future development of Canada as espoused by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). Not that I am suggesting that the statements made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development do not express
his genuine concern about the ecology of the Canadian north. In this regard, I give him full credit. But what assurance have we received that the effect of the total package of government policy will not be a sell-out, again to use a phrase current in 1956, to the "Texas buccaneers"? This is the nub of the question we have to consider when we are expressing our concern about current dangers to all parts of Canada. Does it matter if we preserve our ecology if we do not preserve a viable economy for the benefit of a future generation? To me this is the basic and underlying issue of this debate.
It is apparent that there is an entirely new dimension to this question of the future transportation of petroleum products and the effect on Canadian interests. The ecological dangers have become more and more apparent to all of us. This new dimension has in part become apparent because of the fact that we are considering the exploitation of our resources in areas where the ecology is very different from that which existed in those areas involved in the earlier pipeline debate. This new element of danger is increased by the fact that what is now being done is so much different in degree as to become different in kind as far as its impact on the ecology of this country, the continent and, indeed, the world, is concerned.
We have had discussions which indicate that this is true not only in this area of our economic activity, but also in other areas because of the tremendously increased power to change the whole face of the world, which has become evident since 1956. In the discussions about the trans-Canada gas pipeline a great number of exclamation marks were placed behind the words that we were going to be building a pipeline larger than had ever been built before. It was to be 36 inches in diameter.
As I understand it, and I refer for a moment to the report which appeared in the New York Times of May 3, 1970, the proposed pipeline across Alaska would be four feet in diameter and close to 800 miles long, carrying a deluge of oil through otherwise frigid terrain at a temperature of 150 degrees Fahrenheit, or more. It is suggested in this report:
Secretary Hickel has referred to an above-ground line as a "Chinese Wall". If the pipe were on stilts two feet high and covered with six-inch insulation, it would stand seven feet above the landscape.
These are some of the factors we have to think about when we start talking about an alternative pipeline through Canada. In relation to the concern expressed by the people in British Columbia, we must think not only of where this pipeline will commence but where it will end. I have here a draft statement on environmental matters prepared under the auspices of the Department of the Interior of the United States. This is a preliminary study. I should like to quote briefly from it:
A pipeline route through Canada serving the U.S. Pacific Coast would eliminate the hazards of marine operations only if it is assumed that oil reaching Puget Sound by such a pipeline would continue southward to California by way of a pipeline yet to be proposed. It should he noted, however, that economics heavily favour the movement of oil by ship from Puget Sound to destinations in California. If the decision is made in

March 12, 1971

favor of trans-shipment by water, then any potential hazards of marine terminal operations are merely shifted from Prince William Sound to Puget Sound.
I think one or two of my colleagues may have further observations to make during this debate on this and other related matters.
I noted an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail this morning concerning an interview with Secretary Morton. The report indicates that the Canadian alternative is one into which certain oil companies should be looking. He also suggests that there is very little difference in the ecological dangers involved. A pipeline route to Puget Sound and transportation of oil by tankers from there to California would create the same ecological dangers which would be created by the transportation of oil by tankers from a port in Alaska to Puget Sound. I introduce this point in the debate, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley is not necessarily any quick and easy solution to the problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-OIL-OPPOSITION TO TRANS- ALASKA PIPELINE AND TANKER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR FEASIBILITY STUDY OF ALTERNATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), which reads as follows:
That this House opposes the Trans-Alaska pipeline and tanker project because of the ecological dangers posed by this project to the people, towns, and cities of British Columbia and the national resources of Canada's western seas and coasts and that this House therefore urges the Government to immediately institute an independent economical and ecological feasibility study of alternative routes.
Mr. Speaker, I believe a degree of inconsistency is to be found in the motion. It calls upon the House to oppose the Trans-Alaska pipeline as well as the movement of oil by tanker down Canada's western coast. I really cannot see what other means there is.
Even though a thorough study of the possible consequences of the two alternative routes might be worthwhile, I believe that a pipeline is the best solution. However, before the pipeline is built, approval should be secured from the province or provinces through which it would run and special measures taken to prevent a break that could disturb the ecological balance of the area involved.
I suggest that the government require the builders of the pipeline to hire Canadian workers and use Canadian funds to finance the project.
I do not share the opinion of the hon. member for Peace River who opposes the two solutions already referred to. I am sure that the development of the Alaskan oil industry will very much help our own in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that there are in the Yukon large quantities of unexploited oil, since it is very difficult for companies to make their operations profitable, due to the great difficulty in moving the oil to
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
consumers in large centres. If a pipeline goes through the Yukon, it will be much easier for companies to move the oil to refineries located farther south.
I wish to make a suggestion to the government in connection with that problem. In my opinion, it should study the possibility of having oil refineries built in Canada. If the government authorities were to decide to subsidize adequately those industries, the Americans would probably be interested in having their oil processed in Canada.
I would have many more suggestions to make but I prefer to wait until we know more about this project and how much it will cost.
We, in the Ralliement creditiste, are therefore partly in favour of the motion of the member for Peace River at least as far as the necessary study is concerned and we ask the government to consider seriously the viability of a Trans-Alaska pipeline.
We agree with the NDP on the possibility for Canada to own a pipeline and to set up a corporation which would be the owner since it would facilitate the transportation of our oil to the centres which need it or to the processing plants which would be located where labour is available and the costs lower.
I also suggest that if we owned a pipeline we could propose to the United States to use it against payment of a fee which would ensure the pipeline's viability.

Mr. Speaker, we started to talk about pipelines right after that, and at the beginning of 1969 the Canadian government established a special task force of officials on northern oil development with the duty of looking into the possibility of a pipeline route running through Canadian territory as well as the possibility of tanker routes in the Canadian Arctic. We were quite concerned about all the problems, and our concern was translated into action. We passed legislation to prevent pollution by tankers. Last winter we passed legislation to make sure that if tankers operate in Canadian Arctic waters the environment will be protected. Members of the NDP spoke about that this morning. Even the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) spoke about it. So, Mr. Speaker, I think we have shown our preoccupation with the problem of pollution in the north.
In August last year the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and I issued some guidelines with respect to the construction and development of pipelines in the north. Those guidelines were issued after the task force had recommended that some limitation be placed on the construction of pipelines in the north to make sure that the ecology would be looked after, and to ensure that the native people would benefit from any pipeline construction. Our Canadian native peoples must have a priority with respect to permanent jobs because we believe we must protect their interests. We also stipulated that if there are to be pipelines they must be common carriers so that Canadian interests may use them, even if they are not built by Canadians. In addition, we stipulated that there must be Canadian participation if Canadians themselves want to participate in the development of pipelines.
A lot of people have talked about research, and I have said that we have not yet concluded the research that we have undertaken. In my speech in Dallas, I said that we think eventually there will be pipelines in the north. I
am glad to see that all parties in this House agree that this will be so. The hon. member for Peace River spoke about this prospect, as did the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). I am very happy that the House is behind the government's policies as enunciated by my colleague and I, on the necessity for pipelines in the north.
In Canada, we have done some research. The United States first started by shipping pipe to Alaska, but here in Canada we started by undertaking research. Last year, after we amended the Territorial Lands Act, we established a new program, the ALUR program, which stands for Arctic Land Use Research program. Under it we have hired all sorts of interested people to do research on the protection of the ecology and the effects of pipelines on the permafrost.
Participating in this program are some university people, some Indian people, some Eskimos, and representatives of the oil industry. Right now they are gathering all sorts of useful facts. The Wildlife Service which used to be a part of my responsibility, has also taken part in this work. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis), who now has responsibility for that service, has told me it will continue this work. I am very happy that we will have the benefit of the expertise available in the Wildlife Service, and of the fisheries' research officials who are already studying the effects of northern development on fish in the rivers, and on wildlife in general.
What is important to convey to the House is that the north can benefit immensely from these developments. There will be an investment of some $5 billion if two pipelines are constructed. Of course, there will be problems, but modern technology should be able to solve them. We must make sure that no great amount of pollution is created in the north. I devoted five pages of my speech in Dallas to this topic. Prevention of pollution is one of the conditions we will lay down if application is made to build a pipeline. We must make sure that the northern ecology is protected, and that if pipelines are constructed they will result in minimum damage to the ecology.
We said all these things months ago, Mr. Speaker, and now because we are stressing the Canadian interest some people say we are contradicting ourselves. That is not the case at all. We have a policy which we have spoken about for many months. We have decided we will develop the north and not repeat in the north the errors we have made in the south. This is a commitment we have laid down, not only in speeches but in legislation. As evidence that we are carrying out this commitment, I cite three pieces of legislation passed last year, the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Northern Inland Waters Act, and the amendment to the Territorial Lands Act. While the opposition were sleeping on the topic, we passed those three pieces of legislation.

We must do this because we have disturbed their traditional way of life. Many of them are no longer primarily trappers and hunters. Under our programs many of them are getting the necessary education to enable them to participate in the development of the north. They must have certain priorities with respect to jobs, and I may add that industry is collaborating with us.
Those who say we have not done the research must be blind. There have been numerous newspaper articles printed within the past two years outlining the research we have undertaken. There has been the construction of an experimental pipeline at Iriuvik, where the oil industry is working in collaboration with the government to discover the effect of a hot oil pipeline on the permafrost. The Opposition do not seem to realize that this experiment has been conducted for some two years. I am a bit surprised at that.
Right now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform members of the Opposition, if they have not read the newspapers and have not followed the actions of the government, that at Fort Good Hope an experimental gas pipeline is being constructed to discover the effect of a gas pipeline on the permafrost.
All these things have been done by the industry in collaboration with the government. We do not need confrontation. What we are seeking is balanced development in the north. Mr. Speaker, I am not a doctrinaire person. The NDP members say the pipeline should be built only by Canadians. I have no objection to that if we can find the money here in Canada, but I am not a Social Creditor and I know we don't print money. If we are to spend $5 billion on the construction of a pipeline, we must first discover what the effect will be on other sectors of our economy. Perhaps that is a bit complicated for some. I say that this is a great day for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and for me, because everyone who has spoken in the debate so far seems to have said that we are moving in the right direction. Even the New Democratic Party has supported our idea. I am glad the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said that we were going in the right direction.
Of course, we have not solved all the problems. We need to know more about the ecology and about building
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
pipelines on the permafrost. In my judgment, however, it was advisable to let Canadians and Americans know "that the north is there." Pipelines will be built. If the Americans do not build a pipeline from Alaska I will not be too upset, because I know that we will find enough oil in the future in Canada to justify an oil pipeline. Perhaps it will take two or three years more, but there will be an oil pipeline.
So far as gas is concerned the Americans will have to use the Canadian route if they want a gas pipeline. There is no other way. You cannot ship gas, you must put it through a pipeline. Of course you can liquify it, but that is a very expensive operation. I therefore think that economic factors will force the interests at Prudhoe Bay to use the Canadian route. Since they will build a gas pipeline, perhaps factors of economy will prompt them to build an oil pipeline at the same time. We are not pushing the Americans; we are just putting before them the important fact that the north of Canada is opening and that great amounts of resources are there to be discovered. There is five times more sedimentary rock in the Canadian north than in Alaska. The resources are there; perhaps it will take a few years before we find them. As an example, Panarctic drilled eight wells and made two discoveries of immense proportions. They are major discoveries, perhaps unequalled by any others in the world. I do not think that we could discover gas or oil at the same rate elsewhere, not even in the Middle East. All this indicates a great potential for Canada. We must make sure that these resources go to market, and pipelines are the safest way.

Mr. Speaker, you know these resources are there for the benefit of all Canadians. Last year we passed the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, because we were afraid that technology which could be applied in the Arctic Ocean was not sufficiently advanced to assure safety. That was not an easy decision for us, because we know that there is oil and gas on the Arctic islands. We know, also, that the relevant technology is not far enough advanced for us to be certain of safety. We could not be sure at the time that those tankers would go safely through our Arctic waters. It was for this reason we made that decision. This route is not open and no outline has been given of the conditions under which shipping could take place. The pipelines, however, as compared to tankers, are a different ball game. We know a lot about the technology. Even so, we know that we shall need to devote a great deal more time and research to certain aspects of pipeline building.

March 12, 1971
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
I have talked to the House about some programs we have carried out. I do not yet know when all the research will be completed: I hope it will be finished as soon as possible, but we are not being rushed. We will take all the time we need, because we want to make sure that our pipelines are safe and that our wildlife and tundra in the north do not suffer.
Although I may be preoccupied with the ecology and wildlife, there is one factor that surely cannot escape the attention of members of Parliament. If we build these pipelines in the north, they will benefit the northerners. I am always talking about them. A few months ago when I showed a bit too much sensitivity for the well-being of the tundra in the Mackenzie delta, the Eskimos and Indians of Inuvik protested because they were in danger of losing their jobs with the oil companies. We have to keep all these factors in mind and, of course, make our value judgments. We are trying to do the best that we can.

speechtext:
In the Northwest Territories, the Indians of Fort Good Hope are very happy, because they are working on the experimental pipeline and related activities. These developments in the north will benefit the northerners. We must make plans and make sure that the development in the north helps the people in the north and the people of Canada everywhere.
A few years ago we wanted development at any cost. Today, we have to take other factors into account. We cannot stop development. If we build pipelines in the north, the economic activity will be good for the area; and when there is a good level of economic activity in Canada, all the people of Canada benefit. You know, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the House will recognize that we have accomplished some things in the last three years. I am glad that hon. members realize we must face a challenge. We have been facing it for three years and have done a lot of work on solving it. I hope everyone will appreciate that this House is unanimous today on the question that pipelines have to be built in the north. These pipelines will benefit the Canadian economy and, I hope, especially the native peoples of the north. The pipelines will increase the opportunities for our native peoples. I thank hon. members for allowing me this extension of time to finish my speech.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has been most refreshing. If the motion has done nothing else than elicit some explanation from the minister, it has served a good purpose. I think that we are dealing with a very important subject which must be considered carefully if Canada is to stay one nation for generations to come. The economic decisions that we make now, and the decisions we make about pipelines, will decide not only whether we shall stay together as one nation, but whether we shall remain independent.
For the last two years we have interrogated this government on this subject. We have wanted to know the facts. On what has the government based its studies? May I refer to two speeches that two ministers of this
government have made. One of those, made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) is a very "heavy" speech that was delivered at Denver; the other was made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) at Dallas, Texas. I wish I had time to read the speeches, because one minister took one position and the other took another position.
We have asked about this matter in the question period, because something seemed to be amiss. There has been confusion in the government ranks and ministers have contradicted one another. I, personally, along with other members of my party, have asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources what kind of study he has been making. Do you know what his answer has been, Mr. Speaker? He has said, "We are leaving this to free enterprise." I have examined dozens of answers in Hansard which indicate this position. That has been confirmed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). It is at least refreshing to note that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has listened to the opposition and got on the right wave length. As I say, the other minister said, "We are leaving this to free enterprise." I am a free enterpriser. Nevertheless, in any field in which the parties have interests to accommodate, whether those are the export of crude petroleum to Canada or other interests, those parties will be apt to say what suits them. In this case we are asking people who produce oil on the Prairies, in Alaska and elsewhere, to undertake an independent study which will tell us whether a certain proposed action of theirs will benefit the ecology or the economy of any part of Canada. You are asking people who have a high degree of interest in the answer to undertake a study. I am not criticizing what they might say, because anybody in their position would do the same.
What we are asking for is very simple. We are asking for an independent study to be made by a task force which will look into the ecological and the economic factors and determine what is good for Canada. The minister has said that the government has done a great deal. He told us what the government has done during the last three years. In the meantime, the sections of pipe have been piled up in Alaska. The Americans do not play ducks and drakes. They do not take pipe up there merely because they want to employ their people or keep their ships busy. They have taken pipe up there because they have decided what to do. They did not stockpile all that pipe for nothing.
In the meantime there has been a big finding of crude petroleum on the northern slopes of Alaska. The Americans now see that they can pipe that crude petroleum from the northern slopes of Alaska to Valdez and take it by tanker down the coast of Canada to Seattle or other ports. The minister says, "There is nothing to this; we might come to some decision this fall or next spring". The United States is not going to wait for the vacillation of this government or the contradiction of one minister. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Develop-

March 12, 1971

ment said to the Americans in Dallas that we need their money. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources practically threatened the Americans when speaking in Denver. He said we might even jam their television and radio stations. He said we want to preserve everything for Canadians, even our culture. Never has the cabinet been so divided. I see the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) laughing. He knows I am correct. The success of this government is to be on all sides of all problems at all times so that no matter how attacked, they are always correct. That is really what they are doing.
The next question is why is there urgency? Why is the United States acting now? It is not just for the purpose of immediately developing the industry in Alaska. The facts are these. The outcome of the mid-east oil showdown resulted in quick price boosts which made cheap oil vanish from Europe and Japan. Oil is no longer a cheap commodity. Consumers in Canada and the United States are going to have to pay higher prices for their gasoline. That hard fact is sinking in around the world now that these old, rich countries in the mid-east have won unprecedented price increases. Twenty-three of the world's giant oil firms knuckled down under the pressure of the six countries around the Persian Gulf to increase the price of crude petroleum. The same happened in Venezuela. What happened? The 200 million consumers to the south of us will not pay just any price for gasoline and the byproducts of crude petroleum because of economic developments, so they started to stockpile. They do not have time for our procrastination. They have consumers and therefore have to move.
I hoped that one of the two ministers who spoke today would have stated that negotiations are going on with the United States. The minister did not state that, as a result of discussions, the United States have now decided not to use that pipe. They are going to use the pipe and the tanker. Even with the limited knowledge I have, I would like to see a forum set up like the Borden commission so that we would know how to handle the ecology of the north and everyone would be informed. I agree with the minister that a pipeline through the Mackenzie valley is the answer. The oil line may have to go above the permafrost and the gasoline line underneath. Neither I nor the minister are here to solve these technical problems. These must be solved by experts.
The United States is not going to wait. They have moved the pipe into Alaska. They have billions of barrels of oil in their state of Alaska and intend to move it by tanker to the other 48 states. This is what they are saying to the Canadian government. I hope the government will say that they have made a deal with the United States whereby they have agreed to share the cost of building a pipeline down the Mackenzie valley because of the danger to the ecology and the western coastline. I would be reassured if I heard a statement like that. In fact, I would not even bother speaking today if I could be assured the government made that kind of deal with the United States.
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
I have read the United States world news reports and watched American television programs. They still get into eastern Canada, even though they are jammed out of the west because we must live differently from the people in the east. The feeling is growing that the United States is on the move. They are going to supply gasoline to their consumers at a price that the Americans can afford to pay. That is what this is about. This is not a game, it is an economic problem. I say that we need a study. The problem is that it is two years too late. Tanker oil pollution near Canada's western shoreline, in conjunction with the announced increase price of gasoline, are two of the foremost problems facing Canadians. We cannot divorce oil pollution from unemployment or the economic growth of this nation.
A pipeline could carry crude petroleum from Alaska and Canada's northern Arctic or gas from the Christian Islands, about which the minister spoke. The government talks about 100,000 jobs for Canadians. At a time when we have great unemployment, if we had a plan for a pipeline now this program could be negotiated with the United States. As a result, many Canadians could be put to work. We could negotiate with the United States to use Canadian steel, pipe and workers. This is what was done in connection with the Trans-Canada pipeline. If it had not been for the debate, this would not have happened. The pipe was made in Canada.
What will this do to the central industrial areas in Ontario and Quebec as well as western Canada? The government could work out a plan with the United States to protect the ecology and the economics of this country. All the government has promised has been to continue unemployment and pay the unemployed $100 a week. This keeps taxes at such a high level that it is impossible to even get Canadians interested in purchasing Home Oil. That is wrong. One subject cannot be isolated from the other.
With the increase in the cost of crude petroleum and natural gas throughout the world, the United States intends to get supplies of these resources out if at all possible. That is what is happening. There are two routes, one of which is the route to Valdez and then by tanker. There are now 500,000 ton tankers being built. One spill is all we need. Are the ministers strong enough to tell the United States that they cannot bring tankers down our shoreline to United States ports? I would like to hear a statement like that. I would like to see how we could stop this development if the United States decides to undertake it. It would be very interesting.
In the countries with a high gross national product, the United States, Japan and Germany, they realize they have to pay more for their crude petroleum. A London correspondent wrote and I quote:
The era of cheap oil has ended in the West and cannot be expected to reappear in the foreseeable future.
Has the government told the Canadian consumers in the big cities such as Montreal and Toronto that they are going to be paying more for their gasoline? That is what is going to happen in the very near future. I continue to quote:
4222

March 12, 1971
Trans-Alaska Pipeline
Industry experts here are convinced that the precarious balance between producing and consuming nations has tilted sharply in favour of the producers. From Geneva, this assessment came after talks with some of Europe's top business economists:
Throughout most of the post-war period, especially in the 1960s, Europe has benefited from rapidly expanding imports of low-cost oil from the mid-east and from North Africa. Petroleum surpluses and sharp competition among international oil companies have tended to hold prices low.
Now the picture is sharply changed. European consumption has risen faster than was foreseen. Western Europe now meets well over 50 per cent of its energy requirements from oil and covers more than 85 per cent of its total oil consumption by imports from the mid-east and North Africa.
World oil consumption could double again in the 70s according to estimates prepared by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group. And there is little hope that Europe can reduce its dependence on Arab oil in the next five or ten years.
Bear in mind, too, that these forecasts are based upon relatively stable conditions. All we need is a blow-up in the middle east and we are in trouble. Bearing in mind the obligations and commitments of the United States as the world's leading power, may I ask whether Canada has negotiated with the United States to cover a situation in which the United States was involved in the kind of conflict I have envisaged, and Canada remained neutral? Would oil continue to flow through the pipeline? Are we prepared to guarantee that it would continue to flow under such circumstances? I have no doubt that American business people will ask us these questions.
The minister admits we do not have enough money in Canada to finance these pipeline projects. I agree, and I am glad to hear him say this. I am glad there is one minister in the cabinet who tells the truth. The truth is, we have no choice but to tell the Americans and other foreigners that we need their capital. It is up to us to set guidelines, and that is another story, too. The fact is that the government moves from crisis to crisis, as it did in the case of Home Oil. Today there is no trading in Home Oil shares on the stockmarket as a result of the decision which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has taken. If there is to be an independent study, say so and produce the facts. I would point out that the National Energy Board in whose hands, we gather, the whole industry is to be left, is not properly equipped to handle such situations. Witnesses are called to appear before the Board as if it were engaged in a judicial process. Afterward, decisions are made. If an independent body were set up, working for the national interest, I would think the board itself would make the proper decision when the evidence came before it. But everything has to be worked out in consultation with the United States.
